strings.step.overview.title: Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion (ACDF)
strings.step.overview.body:
Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is a surgical procedure that aims to relieve compression on the spinal cord and stabilize the cervical spine.
ACDF consists of three main procedures: **anterior cervical discectomy**, **interbody cage implantation**, and **anterior cervical fixation**.
Compared with **[posterior cervical decompression and fusion (PCDF)](procedure:pcdf)**, ACDF is performed through a frontal approach, utilizing a small incision in the front of the neck to access the cervical vertebrae.
Owing to this surgical approach, ACDF is particularly effective for treating pathologies involving the **anterior structures** of the cervical spine.

strings.step.indications.title: Indication for ACDF
strings.step.indications.body:
ACDF is commonly performed to treat pathologies involving the **anterior aspect** of the cervical spine.
Common indications include:
- **Cervical radiculopathy** and **myelopathy**
- **Degenerative disc disease**
- **Cervical spondylosis** with **ventral** osteophyte formation
- **Cervical spinal malalignment**
In this 3D model, anterior compression of the spinal cord is demonstrated.
Specifically, a C4–C5 disc herniation with cervical myelopathy is depicted.
This represents a typical clinical scenario in which ACDF may be preferred over a posterior approach, allowing for direct decompression through an anterior surgical corridor.

strings.step.discectomy.title: Anterior Cervical Discectomy
strings.step.discectomy.body:
The first step in ACDF is removing the damaged intervertebral disc, otherwise known as **discectomy**.
The intervertebral disc is a soft, cushion-like structure located between vertebrae.
It acts as a shock absorber, helping the spine withstand movements and mechanical stress.
When a disc herniates, part of the disc bulges outward and presses on the **spinal cord** or **nearby nerves**.
This pressure may cause symptoms such as neck pain, weakness, numbness, or tingling sensation in the upper extremity, or difficulty with balance and coordination.
By removing the herniated disc, the surgeon can relieve pressure on the spinal cord and nerves, often improving these symptoms.
Removing the disc also allows the surgeon to directly access and remove other structures that may be causing compression, such as **bone spurs**.

strings.step.cage_types.title: Types of Interbody Cages
strings.step.cage_types.body:
After discectomy, an **interbody cage** is placed to fill the removed disc space.
Interbody cages can be made from a variety of materials, including:
- Durable **medical-grade plastics**, such as Polyetheretherketone (PEEK)
- **Porous titanium**
- **Structural bone grafts** (allograft or autograft)
Oftentimes, surgeons choose the material of the cage **before** the surgery.
On the other hand, the size of the cage is usually determined **during** the surgery.
Once the discectomy is completed, surgeons manually measure and test the appropriate size of the cages that can adequately replace the removed disc.

strings.step.cage_implantation.title: Interbody Cage Implantation
strings.step.cage_implantation.body:
Once the size of the interbody cage has been determined, it is inserted into the exact space where the disc has been removed.
The role of this instrument is to restore the **disc height**, restore the **alignment** of the cervical spine, and to provide a **scaffold for fusion**.
Interbody cages are designed in a way that, over time, new bone grows **through** or **around** the implant, joining the adjacent vertebrae into a single, stable bone.
It is also designed to **withstand forces** placed on the neck during everyday activities while the bones heal completely.

strings.step.anterior_fixation.title: Anterior Cervical Fixation
strings.step.anterior_fixation.body:
The fusion of the vertebral bones may take between **6 and 12 months**, depending on the extent of the surgery, the patient's comorbidities, and other factors.
Until the vertebrae have fused into a single solid bone, **cervical plate fixation** may be performed.
During this step, a small metal plate, usually made of **titanium**, is attached to the front of the vertebrae with **screws**.
The plate acts as an internal brace, keeping the vertebrae and interbody cage in the correct position while the bones heal.
Depending on the extent of the spinal disorder, the plate may span one or more spinal levels.
In most cases, the plate and screws are intended to remain in the body **permanently**.

strings.step.summary.title: Summary
strings.step.summary.body:
Some of the key features of ACDF are as follows:
- It consists of **anterior cervical discectomy**, **interbody cage implantation**, and **anterior cervical fixation**.
- It is highly effective in treating disorders affecting the **anterior** portion of the spine.
- It uses **interbody cages** and **bone grafts** to promote fusion between adjacent vertebrae.
- The plate and screws are typically intended to remain in place **permanently**, even after bone fusion has occurred.
Owing to these advantages, ACDF remains one of the most performed procedures to relieve compression on the spinal cord and nerves while providing long-term stability to the cervical spine.
